newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: "Go on, sue me," Singapore's Goh tells opposition.
newsitem.headline: "Go on, sue me," Singapore's Goh tells opposition.

text.p: Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong has told an opposition candidate for January 2 elections to go right ahead and sue him over campaign remarks.

Goh said he would go on describing Tang Liang Hong of the Worker's Party as a man threatening racial harmony in Singapore and that Tang's threat of legal action was a ploy to bury the issue, according to lawyers' letters made public on Monday.
Tang had written to Goh and Singapore patriarch Lee Kuan Yew demanding an apology, damages and a promise not to repeat allegations that Tang was a "Chinese chauvinist".
Replies from the two leaders of the People's Action Party (PAP), which has won every election since 1959, challenged Tang to carry out his threat.

"If Mr Tang really believes he has a case, then our client invites Mr Tang to apply immediately for an interim injunction to prevent our client from repeating the same or similar statements," Goh's lawyer wrote.
He and a lawyer for Lee said the remarks were based on fact and were fair comment, valid defences in a defamation suit. Goh was ready to go to court and challenge any action, the letter said.
Goh has repeatedly accused Tang of threatening racial harmony in Singapore, which is nearly 80 percent ethnic Chinese but with significant minorities of Tamils and Malays.
He has accused Tang of complaining more than two years ago that there were many Christians and English-educated ministers and senior bureaucrats.
"So, the implication is, now we are Chinese-educated, we are not Christians, how is it Singapore is being run by Christians," Goh said.
He called Tang "a dangerous character" who "plugs a dangerous line".

One of Singapore's strongest memories is brief racial riots before it split from Malaysia in 1965. The PAP says that in its long years of power, it has forged a meritocracy in which the most able lead and race plays no part.
Goh said Tang's comment risked fuelling a revival of racial tensions.
The Straits Times on Monday quoted Tang as saying he was not sure of the exact words he had used.
"But I have definitely never said anything which concerned anti-Christianity," it quoted him as telling a campaign rally on Sunday night.

It said Tang accused Goh of trying to frighten voters into keeping him out of the 83-member parliament, where the PAP is assured of a continued majority with opposition parties contesting only 36 seats.
"They say if you vote Tang Liang Hong to parliament, there will be riots in Singapore," Tang said.
"What riots? If I had really said those words 2-1/2 years ago, until now have there been any riots?
"But today, PAP, TV, radio and newspapers repeat those words every day. If there is a riot now, who will be responsible. PAP, right?" the newspaper quoted Tang as saying.
